detailed_rationale:
Prism Johnson is a diversified building-materials group spanning cement (Prism Cement), tiles/bathware (H&R Johnson) and ready-mix concrete (RMC). FY26 looked solid at the full-year level: consolidated revenue rose 8.4% to Rs 7,404cr and EBITDA surged 52.1% to Rs 693cr, with cement segment revenue +12.7% (volumes +11.7% YoY, premium-product mix rising to 62% of cement/clinker sales from 46% a year earlier), RMC revenue +9.6% with EBITDA up a strong 37.2%, and tiles/bathware margin improving to 7.3% from 5.8% even on modest 2.3% revenue growth. But Q4 FY26 alone told a different story: net profit collapsed 95% YoY to just Rs 6.4cr (from Rs 129.3cr), driven by genuine operating-margin compression (PBDIT margin excluding other income fell to 8.36% from 10.13%) from rising input costs, competitive cement pricing, and higher employee and interest costs (Rs 40.4cr) - one detailed review found no evidence this was explained by a one-off gain in the prior-year quarter, so we treat the Q4 profit collapse as a genuine (if sharp) margin event tied to industry-wide cement-sector pricing pressure, not primarily an accounting artifact.

Leverage and coverage readings vary meaningfully by source, which is itself worth flagging: our quant feed shows D/E of 1.10 and interest coverage of 3.86x, while an independent review cites D/E of 0.90 and, more concerningly, a five-year average EBIT-to-interest coverage of just 0.47x - a figure that, if accurate on a comparable basis, would imply a chronic, severe debt-service problem across recent years rather than a single weak quarter. We could not independently verify that 0.47x figure's methodology within this pass, so we do not treat it as confirmed, but the divergence itself (a single-digit-times coverage reading from our data versus a sub-1x reading elsewhere) suggests genuine ambiguity about how comfortably this company services its debt through the cycle, which argues for caution rather than benefit of the doubt. Valuation readings also diverge sharply (our PE of 76.6x vs one independent calculation of 326.6x, likely reflecting different EPS bases before/after the Q4 collapse), but every reading agrees the stock is not cheap for a cyclical, margin-volatile building-materials business.
recommendation_rationale: The FY26 full-year segment story (cement premiumisation, RMC margin gains) is genuinely encouraging, but the Q4 profit collapse reflects real, industry-wide margin pressure rather than a one-off distortion, and independent leverage/valuation reads are considerably more concerning than our own quant snapshot on at least one measure each. Given the ambiguity around true through-cycle interest coverage and the agreement across sources that the stock is expensive for a cyclical business, we see no basis to rescue this to Hold.
summary: Prism Johnson's cement and ready-mix businesses grew well over the full year, but the most recent quarter showed a sharp, genuine profit collapse from margin pressure in the cement sector, and independent readings of the company's debt-servicing comfort are more concerning than our own data alone suggests. Given the valuation on offer, we recommend Sell.
positive_para: Full-year FY26 segment performance was genuinely encouraging: cement volumes grew 11.7% with premium mix rising sharply (46% to 62% of sales), RMC EBITDA grew 37.2%, and tiles/bathware margins improved even on modest revenue growth. Long-term debt has also been reduced modestly (Rs 1,065cr to Rs 964cr).
negative_para: Q4 FY26 alone showed a genuine, severe margin collapse (operating margin 10.13% to 8.36%, PAT margin 6.93% to 1.33%) driven by input costs, competitive cement pricing, and rising employee/interest costs - not, as far as we could establish, a one-off base effect. Independent estimates of through-cycle interest coverage (as low as 0.47x on a five-year-average basis, versus our own data's 3.86x) raise real questions about debt-servicing comfort that we could not fully resolve in this pass, and every valuation reading we found - however divergent in magnitude - agrees the stock is expensive for a cyclical building-materials business.
reverse_dcf_judgment: Even on the more conservative of the two PE readings we found (~76.6x), a cyclical, margin-volatile building-materials business with a just-demonstrated severe quarterly margin collapse and ambiguous through-cycle interest coverage does not clear a reverse-DCF at this multiple. Judgment: rich, with added caution flagged around unresolved leverage-metric discrepancies.
